Occurrences.Kwic: 枯木倚寒巖，三冬無暖氣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Teaching Grove of the Lineage Mirror (宗鑑法林), burned-hut case. The source quotes an unnamed hermit comparing himself to a withered tree against a cold cliff with no warmth through three winters; all six attribution rungs leave him unnamed.

ActorAttribution.ActorLabel: the unnamed hermit in the burned-hut case
ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The complete-case speech and narration markers assign the headword-bearing clause to the unnamed hermit in the burned-hut case, as recorded in the attribution note.

Senses.Explanation: A withered or dead tree. Chan speakers use its cold, apparently lifeless condition as a test image, then make it do what such a tree cannot: grow branches, bloom, roar like a lion, or carry hidden news of warmth. Damei Fachang describes himself as a damaged dead tree unchanged by repeated springs; the hermit in the burned-hut case says a dead tree against a cold cliff has no warmth through three winters. Yunfeng Zudeng warns that treating cold ash and dead wood as the old masters' final position falls into a one-color understanding. The phrase therefore keeps the ordinary dead tree visible while public sayings test whether stillness has been mistaken for completion.

Independent biographical records say that Hongzhi Zhengjue first visited or studied under him, and a lineage compilation heads his record as Jingyin Kumu Cheng. This is a person, not a figurative dead tree, so searches and reader links must distinguish the name from the common phrase.

Senses.Explanation: A dead tree flowering joins a tree without living growth to the appearance of blossom. Several Chan speakers direct listeners toward the place where a dead tree flowers or say that discussion can flower there. Yingning Jing and Yunxi Ting use the phrase in praise or verse. The selected witnesses are positive or directional; none of them supplies a warning against 'lodging in deadness.' An unnamed monk in the Continued Lamp Record pairs the dead tree’s flower with welcoming spring before the response that follows.

AlternateTargets: copying another's way and losing one's own
SearchAliases: copying another's way and losing one's own
Senses.Note: This allusive use differs from the actual place and the personal title below. Tang-gait, Handan-gait, imitation, and former-gait variants belong to one walking-imitation family, but their grammatical actors must not be silently interchanged.

Occurrences.Kwic: 清云：邯鄲學唐步。雪竇顯云：這僧不是邯鄲人，為甚學唐步？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Collected Old Cases Raised in the Lineage (宗門拈古彙集), in the comments on Zhaozhou Congshen's tea case: Jingqing Daofu gives the first exact headword verdict after the unnamed monk leaves; Xuedou Chongxian repeats the headword in the immediately following comment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 脚下若參差，邯鄲學唐步。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Complete Book of the Five Lamps, volumes 34–120 (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)): in Xichan Wenlian's explicitly headed section, Xichan Wenlian warns that if one's footing is off, one resembles the Handan walker imitating another gait.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不可在語脈裡轉嫫母效顰邯鄲學步見笑大方取譏識者
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of National Master Puji Yulin (普濟玉琳國師語錄): Yulin Tongxiu warns that examining public cases by turning inside their verbal thread is like the ugly woman imitating a frown or learning the Handan walk, inviting ridicule from knowledgeable people.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打失衲僧鼻孔，忘却邯鄲故步。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Correct Lineage of the Continuation of the Lamp (續燈正統): inside Sanyi Mingyu's explicitly headed small address, Sanyi says that patch-robed monks lose their noses and forget the old Handan gait, then surveys the assembly and says 'exposed.'

Senses.Explanation: A walking-imitation allusion used as a verdict on derivative conduct: someone copies another gait and may lose the step previously his own. The records preserve two grammatical directions rather than one person called a 'Handan gait-imitator.' In the shorter 'learn the Handan gait' (邯鄲學步), attested eight times in seven allowlisted texts, Handan supplies the gait being copied. In the more frequent Chan formula 'Handan learns the Tang gait' (邯鄲學唐步), attested 48 times in 35 texts, a Handan person instead copies a Tang gait. Jingqing Daofu applies the latter verdict when an unnamed monk walks away after being asked how he understands Zhaozhou Congshen's 'drink tea'; Xuedou Chongxian then asks why someone who is not a Handan man learns the Tang gait. Xichan Wenlian attaches the formula to uneven footing, while Yulin Tongxiu warns that following the verbal thread of public cases becomes 'learning the Handan gait' and invites informed ridicule. Sanyi Mingyu speaks of forgetting Handan's former gait. Chan deployment therefore keeps the walking, imitation, and loss-of-one's-own-step scene visible while reversing who copies whom; those grammatical roles do not create separate lexical things.

Senses.Note: This sense covers the place itself, including when a poem invokes the dream located there. It is secondary because the imitation formula dominates the Chan concordance.

Occurrences.Kwic: 妾家邯鄲住，歌聲亦抑揚
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Yi'an (翼菴禪師語錄): in the collected Hanshan poem, Hanshan's poetic voice says that his home is in Handan and his singing rises and falls.

Occurrences.Kwic: 邯鄲一枕，歷盡榮華五十載，覺來黃粱炊尚未熟
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi (百癡禪師語錄): Baichi Yuan, in his inscription on the Record of Lu Sheng's Yellow-Millet Dream (題盧生黃粱夢記), recounts the Handan pillow dream and says that Lu Sheng awoke before the millet was cooked.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs also name the actual city of Handan. One verse says, “my home is in Handan” (妾家邯鄲住). Chan writing also preserves the city as the setting of the yellow-millet dream: “one pillow at Handan: he passed through fifty years of glory; on waking, the yellow millet was not yet cooked” (邯鄲一枕，歷盡榮華五十載，覺來黃粱炊尚未熟). Literal residence and the dream’s setting retain the same geographic referent; the literary allusion does not make a new place.

Senses.Note: One creature. Jar-bound, paired with a well frog or mosquito, and made to swallow an otter are different deployments of the same vinegar gnat, not separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 獨惜其甕裏醯雞，爭知天日？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source text (宗門拈古彙集): A master calls the criticized group gnats inside a jar and asks how they could know the sky and sun. Exact actor: Baiyan Jingfu.

Occurrences.Kwic: 撲破醯雞甕裏天，隨方遊戲莊嚴海。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source text (佛語御禪師語錄): In a fire instruction, the speaker says to smash the sky inside the vinegar gnat's jar and travel freely through the adorned sea. Exact actor: Foyu Yu.

Occurrences.Kwic: 醯雞吞卻黃毛獺
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source text (百愚禪師語錄): A hall address makes the minute vinegar gnat swallow a yellow-furred otter. Exact actor: Baiyu Si.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所以醯雞蚊蚋湊泊之者難，隨他醋甕草窠中經冬度夏
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source text (百癡禪師語錄): A portrait verse says that vinegar gnats and mosquitoes find it hard to approach and lets them pass winter and summer in the grassy nest of a vinegar jar. Exact actor: Baichi Yuan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟道出常情，非井蛙醯雞所能窺測。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source text (朝宗禪師語錄): A letter says that Linji's words pass beyond ordinary sentiment and cannot be peered at or measured by a well frog or vinegar gnat. Exact actor: Chaozong Tongren.

Senses.Explanation: A vinegar gnat is a minute creature repeatedly placed inside a vinegar jar. Baiyan Jingfu calls a group's perspective that of “a gnat inside a jar” and asks how it could know the sky and sun; another fire instruction says to smash the sky inside the vinegar gnat's jar. A portrait verse lets such gnats and mosquitoes pass winter and summer in the vinegar jar's grassy nest. The creature also enters Chan's scale reversals: a hall address has a vinegar gnat swallow a yellow-furred otter. Elsewhere Linji's words are said to pass beyond what a well frog or vinegar gnat can peer at. The jar, restricted sky, minute creature, and impossible swallowing remain one animal referent; the corpus turns it into appraisal, fire-instruction verse, portrait language, and teaching-seat scale reversal. The exact term occurs 41 times in 29 allowlist texts.
